title: Classify the artifact and its identity context
clue: A secret-like value, key file, stored hash, challenge response or ticket
conditions: Artifact provenance and format; possible local/domain/application identity and compatible protocol
access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context
result: A typed credential record with a justified use or recovery path
mechanics: An NT hash, Net-NTLMv2 response and DCC2 verifier are not interchangeable. Source and format constrain cracking mode, reuse protocol and expected rights.
example: Observation: a recovered value is labelled a hash. Test: inspect its format and producing source. Illustrative output: it is a challenge-response capture rather than an NT verifier. Interpretation: choose offline recovery; reject direct Pass-the-Hash.
verify: Identify artifact type, source, account/domain and compatible next operation; record unknowns instead of guessing.
failure: A 32-character hexadecimal value is not enough to identify its algorithm. Use application/source evidence and converters.

recognition.where: Return to the file, database row, capture or session that produced the artifact; inspect structure and account labels before choosing a tool mode.
recognition.sample:
Possible structures:
-----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----
USER::DOMAIN:CHALLENGE:RESPONSE:BLOB
USER:RID:LM_HASH:NT_HASH:::
recognition.spot: Headers and producing context distinguish a private key, challenge response and stored NT verifier.
recognition.confirm: Record the exact source, user/domain and complete format; identify compatible recovery/authentication operations.
recognition.enabled: Source and format agree on the type: route it to the matching recovery/use method.
recognition.ruledout: The value is an application identifier rather than an authentication artifact: reject the credential hypothesis.
recognition.unknown: A bare hexadecimal string without provenance does not identify its algorithm; investigate the producing application.

procedure:
```text
SOURCE -> MATERIAL/FORMAT -> LOCAL/DOMAIN/APPLICATION IDENTITY
-> POSSIBLE USE -> SERVICE/PROTOCOL -> AUTHENTICATION
-> AUTHORIZATION -> NEW ACCESS -> RE-ENUMERATION
```

Record source, claimed identity, format evidence, possible uses, tested service, result and resulting rights together.

| Material | Recognition | Compatible use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cleartext password | Text tied to an identity/source | Normal protocol/application login |
| SSH private key | OpenSSH/PEM private-key block | SSH public-key authentication; recover passphrase offline if protected |
| Linux password record | `USER:$id$salt$digest:...` | Offline recovery with complete record/format |
| Application/file verifier | Tool-specific `$...$` or documented digest | Offline recovery with matching mode/parser |
| NT hash | Usually 32 hex from SAM/LSASS/NTDS context | Offline recovery; PtH where NTLM and the client support it |
| Net-NTLMv2 response | `USER::DOMAIN:challenge:proof:blob` | Offline recovery or live relay under specific conditions; not PtH material |
| DCC2/MSCache v2 | Username-dependent cached-domain verifier | Offline recovery; not ordinary PtH material |
| Kerberos ticket | `.kirbi`, ccache or in-memory cache | Ticket-specific access subject to realm, SPN, validity, clock and route |
| Kerberos roast material | `$krb5asrep$...` or `$krb5tgs$...` | Offline recovery with matching enctype/mode |
| Session/API token | Cookie, bearer/JWT or application token | Issuing application and authorization context only |

Do not feed unknown strings into random modes. Preserve the source and identity context, then identify the format:

```bash
hashid HASH_OR_FILE
john --list=formats | grep -i KEYWORD
hashcat -hh | grep -i KEYWORD
hashcat --example-hashes | less
```

> **Failure cue:** `No hashes loaded`, token/line-length errors or zero parsed hashes normally indicate wrong format, mode, damaged input or unsupported version—not a strong password.

| Output | Type | Immediate compatible possibilities | Not valid as |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cleartext password | Reusable secret | Password authentication, key derivation, DPAPI where applicable | Proof of authorization |
| NT hash | NTLM key | Offline crack; PTH where NTLM/service policy allows; Kerberos RC4 transition where supported | Net-NTLM response or DCC2 |
| AES128/AES256 key | Kerberos long-term key | Request Kerberos material using compatible tooling | Direct NTLM authentication |
| `.kirbi` / ccache | Kerberos ticket container | Use while valid for its client/realm/SPN scope | Password/hash |
| DCC2/MSCache v2 | Offline verifier | Offline cracking | PTH |
| DPAPI key/blob | Protected-data material | Decrypt only with matching context/keys | General logon credential |
| Machine-account key | Computer identity | Map the computer account's rights and Kerberos/NTLM paths | Human/domain-admin identity |

Every newly usable identity returns to Block 10 before movement:

```text
VERIFY MATERIAL -> AUTHENTICATE SAFELY -> CONFIRM IDENTITY
                -> MAP GROUPS/RIGHTS/SHARES/HOSTS/ROUTES
```

title: Validate known passwords and context-specific reuse
clue: A password tied to a plausible user and service
conditions: Correct local/domain/application identity, reachable compatible service, accepted authentication and account state
access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context
result: A verified authentication result followed by tested service-specific authorization
mechanics: One password may belong to several independently managed identities. Authentication success is useful only when associated with a precise service and allowed action.
checks:
```bash
nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD'
ssh -p PORT USER@TARGET
```
example: Observation: a configuration contains a username/password. Test: validate the source application first, then an evidence-backed OS/domain reuse. Illustrative output: SMB authenticates but no administrative access exists. Interpretation: enumerate readable shares rather than assume execution.
verify: Record exact identity, service and tested read/write/session effect; classify authentication and authorization separately.
failure: Account disabled, expired password, wrong domain and denied logon require different responses. Avoid repeating a known-valid password against a denied action.

recognition.where: Use the account label from the producing source and the observed service inventory to choose one compatible, correctly qualified validation.
recognition.sample:
SMB TARGET [+] DOMAIN\USER: accepted
Administrative execution: not yet demonstrated
recognition.spot: Accepted authentication proves one service/account pairing; it does not establish shares, administration, RDP or WinRM.
recognition.confirm: Inspect the actual permitted object/action and account state; consider lockout policy before any broader testing.
recognition.enabled: The intended service operation succeeds under the recorded identity: use that access and re-enumerate.
recognition.ruledout: The secret is valid only for the application and not the proposed OS account: reject that reuse pairing.
recognition.unknown: A generic logon failure may hide account/domain/state mismatch; classify it before repeating attempts.

procedure:
Use the normal client for the observed service: ```bash ssh -o PreferredAuthentications=password -p PORT USER@TARGET nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --shares evil-winrm -i TARGET -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' xfreerdp /v:TARGET /u:'DOMAIN\USER' /p:'PASSWORD' /cert:ignore ``` Local Windows account: ```bash nxc smb TARGET --local-auth -u USER -p 'PASSWORD' --shares ``` > **Decisive output:** the destination service accepts the intended identity. Share, session or action access is a separate authorization result.
Variant — known user, targeted password dictionary ```bash hydra -l USER -P WORDLIST -s PORT -t 4 -f ssh://TARGET hydra -l USER -P WORDLIST -t 1 -f rdp://TARGET ``` Use only on an assigned target after checking lockout and rate controls. Confirm every reported success with the normal client.
Variant — one password across an authorized user list ```bash hydra -L USERS -p 'PASSWORD' -s PORT -t 1 rdp://TARGET nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USERS -p 'PASSWORD' --continue-on-success ``` One attempt per account can still trigger lockout or monitoring. Establish scope, threshold/window and observation period first.
Variant — HTTP POST form Capture a correct request and stable failure marker with Burp: ```bash hydra -l USER -P WORDLIST TARGET http-post-form \ '/LOGIN_PATH:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:F=STABLE_FAILURE_TEXT' ``` Dynamic CSRF tokens, cookies, redirects, throttling and uniform responses require manual handling or a different approach. A weak failure marker creates false positives.
```text accepted identity -> groups/roles -> reachable services -> shares/files -> authenticated application behavior -> accessible hosts/routes -> new credentials/tickets/sessions -> privilege and movement handoffs ``` Verify destination host, accepted identity and actual read/write/execute rights. New hosts/listeners return to discovery; recovered material returns here; operating-system execution enters session handling; domain identities enter AD mapping. ```cmd net accounts /domain ``` ```powershell Get-DomainPolicyData | Select-Object -ExpandProperty SystemAccess ``` Password validation belongs to the existing [credential procedure](https://github.com/ArmaanLeg3nd/OSCP-Exploitation-Reference/blob/main/reference/04-shells-transfers-credentials/03-credential-use-and-cracking.md). Do not spray by default. If explicitly required, account for lockout threshold, duration, observation window and prior failures; use one justified candidate, stop on lockout/rate-limit evidence and preserve successful identities separately.

next.requires: Reachable SMB/RPC; anonymous, guest, local or domain context must be explicit; share and filesystem ACLs both matter

title: Recover passwords with feasible dictionary, rule and mask attacks
clue: A supported stored verifier or converted protected artifact
conditions: Correct format/mode, complete salt/context, justified candidates and an available offline tool/backend
access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context
result: A recovered candidate password or a documented exhausted search strategy
mechanics: Offline cracking compares candidate-derived values without contacting the service. Dictionary rules and masks model likely structure; infeasible keyspaces do not become useful through a different tool name.
example: Observation: a supported verifier and a naming/password-pattern clue exist. Test: validate the mode with a known-format sample and apply a focused rule strategy. Illustrative output: one candidate recovers the verifier. Interpretation: verify it against the intended identity/service.
verify: Use the tool's show/result output and then validate the recovered credential in its correct context.
failure: Token/separator errors imply wrong or incomplete input; no recovery means only the tested candidate space was exhausted.

recognition.where: Identify a supported verifier/converter and build candidate structure from relevant names/policy/context rather than selecting an arbitrary hash mode.
recognition.sample:
Artifact format matches SUPPORTED_MODE
Candidate model: relevant words plus a justified suffix pattern
recognition.spot: A verified format and feasible candidate model enable offline recovery; a hash-shaped string alone does not.
recognition.confirm: Check complete salt/context, conversion correctness, tool backend and whether all required factors are present.
recognition.enabled: The verifier and candidate space are valid: use the selected offline strategy and verify recovered credentials.
recognition.ruledout: The artifact is a non-crackable token or unsupported format under this workflow: reject that mode.
recognition.unknown: Parsing errors or an incomplete source require input repair; no recovery only exhausts the tested candidates.

procedure:
```bash hashcat -b -m MODE python3 -c "print((CHARSET_SIZE ** LENGTH) / GUESSES_PER_SECOND)" ``` Use the actual mode and hardware rate. Salts prevent reusable precomputation; iterations and memory-hard KDFs reduce guesses per second. Prefer candidates in this order: ```text exact recovered/default candidates -> organization/user/product words -> observed policy and mutations -> small dictionary plus rules -> known mask/hybrid -> broader curated lists/rules -> exhaustive search only when its measured cost is defensible ``` Preview mutations before spending the candidate budget: ```bash hashcat -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule --stdout wordlist.txt | head -n 50 john --wordlist=wordlist.txt --rules=Jumbo --stdout | head -n 50 ``` ```bash hashcat -a 0 -m MODE hashes.txt wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule --session job hashcat -m MODE hashes.txt --show ``` > `-a 0` is dictionary mode. Do not use `-a 3` with a wordlist; attack mode 3 expects a mask. Common source examples identify NTLM as mode `1000`, Net-NTLMv2 as `5600` and KeePass as `13400`, but confirm against the installed version: ```bash hashcat -h | grep -Ei 'NTLM|NetNTLMv2|KeePass|OpenSSH' ```
Mask and session variants ```bash hashcat -m MODE hashes.txt -a 3 '?u?l?l?l?l?d?d?d' --session targeted-mask hashcat --session targeted-mask --restore ``` > Mask order is a hypothesis about structure. Estimate its keyspace before committing time.
Hybrid variant — base word plus three digits ```bash hashcat -a 6 -m MODE hashes.txt wordlist.txt '?d?d?d' --session targeted-hybrid ``` Use only when evidence supports both the base words and suffix shape.

result: An opened vault or a valid recovered database password

title: Inspect and recover SSH private-key access
clue: A private key from a file read, share, repository or home directory
conditions: Correct key format, passphrase if encrypted, matching server account/key authorization and accepted algorithm/policy
access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context
result: A usable key and a verified SSH authentication context
mechanics: A private-key passphrase protects the file locally; it is not the remote account password. Server acceptance still depends on user, authorized key, ownership and SSH policy.
example: Observation: a key parser requests a passphrase. Test: recover its protection using the linked converter procedure, then authenticate as the evidence-backed user. Illustrative output: the key decrypts but the server rejects that username. Interpretation: revisit account mapping rather than cracking again.
verify: Verify the key parses and an SSH authentication/session succeeds under the correct target identity.
failure: Invalid format, line endings, wrong passphrase and server rejection are separate layers.

recognition.where: Trace readable key files from home/configuration/backups to a specific username; inspect the key parser's response before testing the server.
recognition.sample:
KEY: OpenSSH private key
Enter passphrase for KEY:
recognition.spot: The artifact is a private key protected by a local passphrase; this is separate from the SSH account password.
recognition.confirm: Determine the protecting passphrase, associated remote user, accepted algorithm and server key authorization.
recognition.enabled: The key parses and the correct server account accepts it: use its permitted shell/subsystem/forwarding capability.
recognition.ruledout: The artifact contains only a public key: reject private-key authentication with that file.
recognition.unknown: A decrypted key rejected by the server leaves username/authorization/policy unresolved.

procedure:
```bash ssh2john id_rsa > ssh.hash john --wordlist=wordlist.txt ssh.hash john --show ssh.hash chmod 600 id_rsa ssh-keygen -y -f id_rsa > derived.pub ssh -vv -i id_rsa -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -p PORT USER@TARGET ``` > Cracking a key passphrase unlocks the file; it does not prove the matching public key is authorized. `Permission denied (publickey)` can mean wrong user/server, missing authorization or server algorithm/policy after a successful local unlock.
Hashcat variant — only for a supported OpenSSH format ```bash hashcat -hh | grep -i 'OpenSSH\|Private Key' hashcat -a 0 -m MODE ssh.hash wordlist.txt -r RULE_FILE ``` Choose `MODE` from the complete `$sshng$...` structure and installed help. Token-length or unsupported-cipher errors require a compatible parser/tool, not `--force` with a wrong mode.

title: Recover Linux account passwords from matched records
clue: Readable password verifiers and account metadata
conditions: Correct passwd/shadow pairing or known hash format; account identity and a feasible recovery strategy
access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context
result: A recovered local account password with a justified privilege/reuse test
mechanics: The verifier encodes algorithm and salt; passwd metadata maps it to a user. Reading a verifier does not itself change UID or authorize sudo.

verify: Tie the recovered password to the correct user and validate an allowed login/sudo transition.
failure: Mismatched snapshots or locked/expired accounts can defeat use even after recovery; inspect account state.

title: Recover or reuse an NT password hash
clue: An NT verifier from an appropriate credential source
conditions: Correct account/domain and actual NT hash; recovery mode or an accepting NTLM service with required destination rights
access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context
result: A recovered password or a verified hash-backed authentication capability
mechanics: Pass-the-Hash uses a long-term NT key in an NTLM exchange; it does not convert every captured hash-like value into a reusable password equivalent.
checks:
```bash
hashcat -m 1000 hashes.txt WORDLIST
nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -H HASH
```
example: Observation: a matched SAM/SYSTEM extraction yields a local NT hash. Test: qualify the target-local identity for one reachable service. Illustrative output: authentication succeeds but execution is denied. Interpretation: record valid authentication and investigate effective rights.
verify: Verify source/type, identity context and the exact permitted service action.
failure: Local/domain confusion, remote UAC and denied NTLM are different from an invalid hash. Use tickets only when their own prerequisites exist.

recognition.where: Inspect the output schema of a justified local/domain credential source, keeping RID, machine and domain labels.
recognition.sample:
USER:RID:LM_HASH:NT_HASH:::
Source: matched local registry extraction
recognition.spot: The source and record fields identify an NT verifier for that local account, not a captured challenge response.
recognition.confirm: Verify the actual NT field, account scope and an accepting service/client with the required destination right.
recognition.enabled: A compatible service accepts the correctly qualified hash identity: use only its verified authorization.
recognition.ruledout: The source produced Net-NTLMv2 or DCC2 instead: reject direct NT-hash reuse.
recognition.unknown: An unlabeled hexadecimal value remains unknown until the source/account is resolved.

procedure:
Offline recovery: ```bash hashcat -a 0 -m 1000 nt.hash wordlist.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule john --format=NT --wordlist=wordlist.txt nt.hash ``` Compatible SMB validation: ```bash nxc smb TARGET -d DOMAIN -u USER -H NT_HASH --shares smbclient //TARGET/SHARE -U 'DOMAIN\USER' --pw-nt-hash NT_HASH ``` > NT hashes come from a producing context such as SAM, LSASS or NTDS. A visually similar 32-hex application digest is not PtH material.
Variant — remote access/execution when the identity has matching rights ```bash impacket-wmiexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' impacket-psexec -hashes :NT_HASH 'DOMAIN/USER@TARGET' xfreerdp /v:TARGET /u:'DOMAIN\USER' /pth:NT_HASH /cert:ignore ``` WMI needs administrative rights plus DCOM/RPC/SMB reachability and normally runs as the authenticated user. PsExec-style execution needs service-control and writable-share rights and commonly yields SYSTEM. RDP hash authentication depends on target/client support and policy. Detailed method selection belongs to the lateral-movement procedure.

title: Recover a password from cached domain logon verifiers
clue: A DCC2/MSCache record from matched SECURITY/SYSTEM material
conditions: Correct username/salt/iteration context and feasible offline candidates
access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context
result: A recovered domain password, subject to current account state
mechanics: Cached interactive-logon verifiers support offline logon checks; they are not reusable NT hashes. Their derivation makes cracking materially different from NT recovery.
example: Observation: cached domain data is extracted. Test: classify it before selecting a tool mode. Illustrative output: DCC2 is identified and one password is recovered. Interpretation: validate against the live domain; the cached value may be stale.
verify: Confirm artifact format, account mapping and current password acceptance.
failure: No recovery does not disprove account existence; stale cached credentials may fail current online authentication.

recognition.where: Inspect SECURITY/SYSTEM parser output and distinguish cached-domain logon verifiers from local SAM hashes and service secrets.
recognition.spot: The DCC2 structure and username-associated derivation identify offline cached-logon material.
recognition.confirm: Verify iteration/username context, source consistency and current online account state after any recovery.
recognition.enabled: A complete supported record and feasible candidates enable the DCC2 recovery workflow.
recognition.ruledout: DCC2 is not accepted directly as an NTLM long-term hash: reject that reuse route.
recognition.unknown: A recovered old password may be stale; validate current account acceptance without assuming extraction failed.

procedure:
```bash
hashcat -hh | grep -i 'Domain Cached'
john --format=mscash2 --wordlist=wordlist.txt dcc2.hash
```

> Preserve the username because it participates in the verifier. DCC2 is an offline recovery target, not ordinary PtH material.

title: Classify tickets and use a compatible cache
clue: A ccache/kirbi file or an existing ticket cache
conditions: Correct principal/realm, valid lifetime, service scope, compatible cache format and naming/KDC route
access: A credential artifact with a recorded source and possible account context
result: A verified Kerberos authentication capability for an appropriate service
mechanics: A TGT can request service tickets; a TGS is scoped to a service/SPN. A ticket for CIFS cannot simply be used as a WinRM credential.
example: Observation: a cache contains a CIFS ticket but no TGT. Test: inspect client/server principals and lifetime. Illustrative output: the target CIFS SPN matches. Interpretation: choose a compatible SMB client, not an arbitrary remote service.
verify: Inspect principal, ticket service, realm and lifetime, then verify the actual service action.
failure: Expired tickets, wrong hostname/SPN, cache format and time skew require different fixes; an IP-only connection can break correct Kerberos naming.

recognition.where: Inspect an existing ticket/cache before collecting new material; identify its client, service, realm and validity.
recognition.sample:
Default principal: USER@REALM
Service principal: cifs/TARGET_HOST@REALM
No krbtgt ticket listed
recognition.spot: This is service-scoped CIFS material, not a TGT for requesting arbitrary services.
recognition.confirm: Check lifetime, cache format, exact SPN/name, route and destination object authorization.
recognition.enabled: The matching SMB service accepts the ticket and allowed operation: use that scoped capability.
recognition.ruledout: A CIFS-only ticket does not enable a WinRM-specific authentication path.
recognition.unknown: An unreadable/expired cache or unknown principal requires inspection/conversion rather than guessed reuse.

procedure:
Inspect before use:

```bash
klist
KRB5CCNAME=TICKET.ccache klist
impacket-ticketConverter TICKET.kirbi TICKET.ccache
```

Compatible client example:

```bash
export KRB5CCNAME=TICKET.ccache
impacket-wmiexec -k -no-pass 'DOMAIN/USER@HOST.DOMAIN'
```

> Verify client principal, realm, TGT versus service ticket, SPN, start/end time, clock, DNS/FQDN and routes. A readable cache does not prove authorization. Roasting, forging and detailed PtT/overpass belong to the AD procedures.
